title: Sharp coherent error from approximate basis-column guarantees
author: /root/batch2_phase
question:
Let \(N\geq1\), let \(\mathcal H\) be a finite-dimensional complex Hilbert space, and let \(U,V:\mathbb C^N\to\mathcal H\) be isometries: \(U^\dagger U=V^\dagger V=I_N\). Their columns include the complete output, including all work registers; no measurement, postselection, or trace-out occurs. Let \(e_0,\ldots,e_{N-1}\) be the standard input basis and suppose exact representative-wise guarantees
\[
\|(V-U)e_j\|_2\leq\varepsilon_j,\qquad \varepsilon_j\geq0,
\]
are known separately for every basis input. All operator norms below are induced Euclidean norms; no minimization over global phase is built into this promise.

Put \(E=V-U\) and \(G_{jk}=\langle Ee_j,Ee_k\rangle\), using an inner product conjugate-linear in its first argument. Derive the exact quadratic form for the error on an arbitrary coherent unit input and the resulting characterization of \(\|E\|\) in terms of \(G\). Decide whether the column guarantees alone imply the dimension-free bound \(\|E\|\leq\max_j\varepsilon_j\). Find the sharp universal bound obtainable from the whole vector \((\varepsilon_j)_j\), including the isometry cap, and prove sharpness for EVERY choice of these nonnegative tolerances by constructing square unitaries on \(\mathbb C^N\). An arbitrary unconstrained error matrix is not a sufficient sharpness witness. Derive the uniform-tolerance corollary and identify when the cap takes over.

For \(N\geq2\), give an explicit family of unitaries whose error on every computational-basis input tends to zero as \(N\) grows while their operator distance stays maximal. A saturating input that changes only by an overall sign does not by itself demonstrate operational distinguishability: also give a normalized superposition on which the intended and actual output states are orthogonal, with a specified distinguishing measurement. Report both the Euclidean vector distance and the trace distance \(\tfrac12\|\rho-\sigma\|_1\) for this latter input, and explain why the first saturating input has different physical-state behavior.

Finally state what additional error-geometry condition WOULD yield a dimension-free bound from the same column norms, and justify it using \(G\). Explain briefly why an explicitly retained orthogonal branch label can supply that condition for controlled branch outputs, whereas linearity by itself does not. This comparison is only a boundary explanation, not a request to re-prove general controlled-family phase correction. Cover zero tolerances, \(N=1\), and exact column agreement. Do not replace full-output Euclidean promises by per-input probability agreement, phase-quotiented agreement, or entrywise matrix error.
assumptions: U and V are isometries on a common N-dimensional input and a common finite complex output space.
Every epsilon_j is nonnegative and bounds the Euclidean difference of the specified full-output column representatives.
conventions: The inner product is conjugate-linear in its first argument, G=E-dagger E, and coherent input coefficients are column vectors.
Operator error is the induced Euclidean norm without a global-phase quotient; trace distance uses one-half the trace norm.

mathematical_target: Sharp nonuniform full-basis-column-to-operator error theorem, attained by legal square unitaries for every tolerance vector, plus an orthogonal-output interference witness.
reference_answer:
For a column coefficient vector \(c\in\mathbb C^N\), linearity gives \(Ec=\sum_j c_jEe_j\). With the stated inner-product convention,
\[
\|Ec\|_2^2=\sum_{j,k}\overline{c_j}c_k\langle Ee_j,Ee_k\rangle
=c^\dagger Gc,
\qquad G=E^\dagger E.
\]
Thus G is Hermitian positive semidefinite, its diagonal is \(G_{jj}=\|Ee_j\|_2^2\), and finite-dimensional spectral theory gives
\[
\|E\|^2=\max_{\|c\|_2=1}c^\dagger Gc=\lambda_{\max}(G).
\]
One may also expand the isometry identities to obtain \(G=2I-U^\dagger V-V^\dagger U\). The off-diagonal entries record coherent correlations of error vectors. Orthogonality of the columns of U and of V separately does not force the columns of their difference to be orthogonal.

Put \(r=(\sum_j\varepsilon_j^2)^{1/2}\). For every unit c, triangle inequality and scalar Cauchy-Schwarz give
\[
\|Ec\|_2\leq\sum_j|c_j|\|Ee_j\|_2
\leq\sum_j|c_j|\varepsilon_j\leq r.
\]
Equivalently \(\lambda_{\max}(G)\leq\operatorname{tr}G\leq r^2\). Since U and V are isometries, \(\|Uc\|_2=\|Vc\|_2=1\), so \(\|Ec\|_2\leq2\). Hence the universal bound is
\[
\boxed{\ \|V-U\|\leq\min\!\left\{2,\sqrt{\sum_j\varepsilon_j^2}\right\}.\ }
\]
There is no statistical-independence assumption or cancellation premise in this estimate.

Here is sharpness even among square unitaries, for each fixed nonnegative tolerance vector. If \(r=0\), choose \(U=V=I\); the zero upper bound is attained. If \(r>0\), define the real nonnegative unit vector \(s=\sum_j(\varepsilon_j/r)e_j\), its rank-one orthogonal projector \(P=|s\rangle\langle s|\), and \(\kappa=\min(2,r)\). Choose a real \(\theta\in[0,\pi]\) such that \(|e^{i\theta}-1|=\kappa\), for example \(\theta=2\arcsin(\kappa/2)\). Set
\[
U=I,\qquad V=I+(e^{i\theta}-1)P=(I-P)+e^{i\theta}P.
\]
The two orthogonal sectors \(\operatorname{ran}P\) and \(\ker P\) receive unit-modulus eigenvalues, so \(V^\dagger V=I\). More explicitly, the mixed products vanish because \(P(I-P)=0\), and both sector products sum to I. Moreover
\[
\|(V-I)e_j\|_2
=\kappa|\langle s,e_j\rangle|
=\kappa\frac{\varepsilon_j}{r}\leq\varepsilon_j,
\qquad \|V-I\|=\kappa\|P\|=\kappa.
\]
The inequality uses \(\kappa\leq r\). Thus the claimed bound cannot be decreased using only those column tolerances, even with full unitarity imposed. For \(r\leq2\), all specified column bounds are attained simultaneously; for \(r>2\), they remain valid upper bounds while the unitary cap is attained. Zero components of the tolerance vector create zero components of s and exactly zero corresponding column errors.

For a uniform tolerance \(\varepsilon_j=\varepsilon\), this reduces to
\[
\|V-U\|\leq\min\{2,\sqrt N\,\varepsilon\},
\]
with transition at \(\varepsilon=2/\sqrt N\). For \(N>1\) the dimension-free assertion \(\|E\|\leq\max_j\varepsilon_j\) is false in general. It is sometimes true for particular error geometry or loose tolerances; the counterexample refutes the universal implication, not every instance.

For a concrete operational witness, take \(N\geq2\),
\[
s=N^{-1/2}\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}e_j,\qquad
U=I,\qquad V=I-2|s\rangle\langle s|.
\]
Then \(V^\dagger V=I\), every column error is exactly \(2/\sqrt N\), and \(\|V-I\|=2\). The column errors tend to zero as N increases, including along qubit dimensions \(N=2^n\). On the saturating input s, the actual output is \(-s\). The vector distance is 2 but the two density matrices are identical, so their trace distance is 0: this input alone detects the chosen representative convention, not an operationally distinguishable physical state.

Now define \(t=(e_0-e_1)/\sqrt2\); it is a unit vector orthogonal to s. For the normalized input \(h=(s+t)/\sqrt2\),
\[
Uh=h=\frac{s+t}{\sqrt2},\qquad
Vh=k=\frac{-s+t}{\sqrt2},\qquad
\langle h,k\rangle=0.
\]
The vector difference is \(-\sqrt2s\), of norm \(\sqrt2\). With \(\rho=|h\rangle\langle h|\) and \(\sigma=|k\rangle\langle k|\), the difference has eigenvalue +1 on h, -1 on k and zero on their orthogonal complement. Therefore \(\|\rho-\sigma\|_1=2\) and the stipulated trace distance is 1. The projective measurement \(\{|h\rangle\langle h|,I-|h\rangle\langle h|\}\) returns its first outcome with probabilities 1 and 0. This establishes a fully distinguishable coherent-output failure despite small errors on every basis input.

The exact additional condition for a desired bound \(\|E\|\leq b\), \(b\geq0\), is \(G\preceq b^2I\). A concrete sufficient geometry for \(b=\max_j\varepsilon_j\) is pairwise orthogonality of the error columns: then G is diagonal and
\[
\|E\|=\max_j\|Ee_j\|_2\leq\max_j\varepsilon_j.
\]
In an explicitly label-preserving controlled comparison, differences of the form \(|j\rangle\otimes(v_j-u_j)\) are orthogonal for distinct j because the labels are orthogonal. That is an additional output interface. It does not follow merely by writing a coherent input as a linear combination. In the present reflection witness all error columns point in the same direction s, which is precisely the opposite geometry. The controlled-label comparison therefore does not contradict the sharp square-unitary result and supplies no free extra label or workspace cleanup.

If every tolerance is zero, exact equality on the entire input basis gives E=0 by linearity. Individual zero tolerances force only their own columns to agree. At \(N=1\), \(\min(2,\varepsilon_0)\) is still sharp for square unitaries, using a scalar phase. The reflection-interference example requires \(N\geq2\); in the one-dimensional square case all unitary output vectors differ only by global phase, although the representative-wise operator distance can be nonzero. Isometries into a larger output space remain covered by the bound but need not share that one-dimensional physical equivalence. No output phase is independently optimized for each input in this problem, and probability agreement is not the stated hypothesis. The proof concerns full columns, not scalar entrywise errors, and derives no circuit realization or oracle cost.

rubric.criterion: Derives the conjugation-correct quadratic form, PSD Gram matrix and largest-eigenvalue characterization; identifies off-diagonal error correlations rather than assuming errors orthogonal.
Proves min(2,sqrt(sum epsilon_j^2)) using all column promises and the isometry cap, and states the sharp uniform sqrt(N) consequence and cap threshold.

Constructs and verifies square unitaries attaining the bound for EVERY nonnegative tolerance vector, with r=0 separated, each column promise checked, and both r<=2 and r>2 handled. An arbitrary unconstrained matrix or only a uniform example earns partial credit.

Provides the uniform rank-one reflection and an explicit orthogonal complement t; computes the distinguishable interference outputs, vector distance sqrt2, half-trace-norm distance 1 and a measurement, while correctly separating the global-sign input's physical trace distance 0.

Gives a sufficient error-geometry condition such as orthogonal error columns, justified by the Gram matrix, and explains the retained-label boundary without pretending linearity supplies the extra output label.

Handles zero tolerances and N=1, preserves complete-output/representative-wise assumptions and the distinction from entrywise or probability promises; no circuit or cleanup resource claim is inferred.

common_errors: Using max_j epsilon_j without controlling cross-column error correlations.
Assuming orthonormal columns of U and V make the difference columns orthogonal.
Using an arbitrary error matrix to claim sharpness while failing the unitary/isometry premises.
Omitting the norm-two isometry cap or dividing by r when all tolerances vanish.
Offering only an overall-sign input as a physical distinguishability witness.
Confusing vector distance 2, vector distance sqrt2, trace norm 2 and trace distance 1.
Silently weakening the full-output Euclidean guarantee to measurement probabilities or independently chosen column phases.
Counting the retained-label orthogonality comparison or the existing entrywise N-epsilon example as the new assessed result.

boundary_cases.consequence: Every error column is zero, so E=0; choose identical unitaries without normalizing an absent direction.
Those columns agree exactly; the rank-one saturating vector has zero corresponding components.
The norm-two isometry cap is active; sharpness need only satisfy, not saturate, each loose column tolerance.
The numerical bound is still sharp by scalar phases; the square one-dimensional case has no two-sector interference witness.
They can force orthogonal error columns, an additional interface absent from general square-unitary comparisons.
A different hypothesis; the reference-wise Gram argument cannot silently adopt it.

steps.claim: The complete coherent error is a Gram quadratic form.
steps.justification: Expand linearity with conjugation in the first argument; maximize the Hermitian quadratic form.

steps.claim: Column data give an l2 aggregate bound while isometry gives the cap.
steps.justification: Triangle plus Cauchy-Schwarz gives r; both outputs of a unit input have norm one, giving 2.

steps.claim: Legal square unitaries saturate every tolerance vector by a case split.
steps.conclusion: At r=0 use U=V=I. For r>0, P=|s><s| with s_j=epsilon_j/r and V=I+(exp(i theta)-1)P, |exp(i theta)-1|=min(2,r), attain the bound.
steps.justification: First separate r=0. In the r>0 branch, orthogonal P/I-P sectors prove unitarity AND individual column calculations prove each promised inequality; division occurs only there.

steps.claim: Uniform promises incur the sharp square-root-dimension factor.
steps.conclusion: Uniform bound min(2,sqrt(N) epsilon), sharp; cap threshold 2/sqrt(N).
steps.justification: Specialize the nonuniform theorem, with the zero case handled separately.

steps.claim: A reflection has vanishing basis-column errors and maximal operator distance.
assumptions: Use N>=2 for the subsequent interference example.
steps.conclusion: For uniform s, V=I-2|s><s| has column errors 2/sqrt(N), operator norm difference 2.
steps.justification: Apply the rank-one projector formula at theta=pi.

steps.claim: The operational counterexample is not merely a global-sign witness.
assumptions: N>=2 as in S5; do not apply this construction at N=1.
steps.conclusion: s maps to -s with trace distance 0; h=(s+t)/sqrt2 maps to k=(-s+t)/sqrt2 orthogonal to h, vector distance sqrt2 and trace distance 1.
steps.justification: t=(e0-e1)/sqrt2 is unit and orthogonal to s; compute inner products AND eigenvalues of |h><h|-|k><k|; a projection onto h distinguishes perfectly.

steps.claim: Orthogonal error columns are a sufficient additional geometry.
steps.conclusion: Diagonal G gives ||E||=max_j||Ee_j||; generally G<=b^2 I iff ||E||<=b.
steps.justification: Spectral order bounds the quadratic form; an explicit retained label forces cross-error inner products to vanish.

steps.claim: Zero and one-dimensional cases preserve the exact quantifiers.
assumptions: The r=0 branch excludes division by r in S3; the N=1 branch excludes the N>=2 witness S5-S6.
steps.conclusion: r=0 implies E=0 and is attained by U=V=I; N=1 still has the scalar-phase sharp cap, but no orthogonal t in the square one-dimensional output.
steps.justification: Linearity extends zero columns; for N=1 the unitary is a scalar phase, distinct from larger-output isometries.
